title: 第十二章王成第二章画皮第十三章鬼母
lines: 第十二章王成
宋焘看完《促织》，在窗前坐了很久。月光从窗外照进来，落在天书上，书页泛着淡淡的银光。他想成安，想那只蟋蟀，想那缕散在父亲掌心的烟。他想了很久，想到月亮西沉，想到天边泛白。最后他闭上眼睛，睡着了。
他做了一个梦。梦里他站在一条大河边上，河水很宽，看不到对岸。河面上漂着许多东西——有纸船，有灯笼，有散了架的书。他蹲下来，伸手去捞一张漂过来的纸。纸上写着字，墨迹模糊，勉强能认出几个：“王成，平原人，性懒，家贫。”
他还没看清，纸就被水冲走了。他站起来，往上游看。河的上游站着一个老人，穿着一件破旧的长衫，头发花白，背微驼，手里拿着一支笔——不是毛笔，是一支很细的、像是骨头做的笔。老人低着头，在河面上写字。他写一个字，河水就翻一个浪，把那个字推向下游。
宋焘想走过去，脚却动不了。他张嘴想问，嘴里发不出声音。老人忽然抬起头，看了他一眼。那一眼，宋焘觉得自己被看透了。不是被看穿了心思，而是被看见了所有——他看过的每一个故事，写下的每一笔天书，都被那个老人看见了。像是一本书被翻到了最后一页，然后合上了。
老人没有说话，低头继续写字。宋焘站在岸边，看着那些字从上游漂下来，一个一个，密密麻麻，挤在一起，像一群鱼在争食。他看见了一个名字——王成。他伸手去捞，抓住了那张纸。纸是湿的，字迹模糊，但他看清楚了。
他睁开眼睛。天已经亮了。他趴在桌上，脸上全是泪。他低头看天书，书翻开了，停在新的一页。
这一章，叫《王成》。
平原县有个闲汉，叫王成。此人原是世家子弟，祖上做过大官，家底殷实。但王成生性懒惰，不善经营，偌大的家业被他败得精光。到了他这一辈，只剩下几间破屋、几亩薄田，连吃饭都成问题。王成又懒又穷，却不思悔改，每天睡到日上三竿才起来，起来也不做事，只是坐在门口晒太阳，看街上的行人来来往往。邻居们都说，王成这辈子完了。
王成不在乎。他爹娘死得早，没人管他，他想怎么活就怎么活。饿一顿饱一顿，日子过得像流水一样，一天一天地淌，没什么盼头，也没什么愁头。
这一年夏天，王成在村里待不住了。他穷得连粥都喝不上了，只好去投奔远方的亲戚。他有个姑妈，嫁在金陵，早年守寡，家境尚可。王成想着去投靠姑妈，好歹混口饭吃。他收拾了一个包袱，把仅有的几件衣裳塞进去，又揣了几个干粮，上了路。
走了三天，走到半路，天黑了。前不着村后不着店，王成只好在路边的一座破庙里歇脚。他进了庙，找了一块干净的地方，铺开包袱，躺下来。刚要睡着，忽然听见门外有声音——“窸窸窣窣”的，像是有人在翻东西。
他爬起来，趴在门缝里往外看。月光下，一个人蹲在墙根，正在翻一堆破砖烂瓦。那人翻了一阵，从砖缝里摸出一串铜钱，数了数，揣进怀里，又蹲下去继续翻。
王成推开门，走了出去。那人听见动静，吓了一跳，站起来就要跑。王成喊住他：“兄台，别跑。我不是坏人。”
那人停下来，回过头，看了他一眼。是个年轻人，二十出头，穿着破旧的衣裳，面黄肌瘦，像个叫花子。
“你是过路的？”那人问。
“是。”王成说，“去金陵投亲。你呢？”
那人叹了口气，说：“我也是去金陵投亲的。走了一天，没吃东西，饿得慌。刚才在这墙根底下翻出几文钱，想去买点吃的。”
王成心里一酸，从包袱里摸出一个干粮，递过去。“吃吧。”
那人愣了一下，接过干粮，狼吞虎咽地吃了。吃完，抹了抹嘴，说：“兄台，你是个好人。我叫李生，也是平原人。咱们同路，不如结伴而行？”
王成答应了。两人在庙里睡了一夜，第二天一早起来，继续赶路。
走了五天，到了金陵。王成找到姑妈家，姑妈见了他，又惊又喜。她拉着王成的手，上上下下地打量，说：“成儿，你怎么瘦成这样？是不是在家吃不饱？”
王成不好意思说，低着头不吭声。姑妈叹了口气，给他收拾了一间房，让他住下。王成在姑妈家住了几天，姑妈对他很好，每天给他做好吃的，还给他做了几件新衣裳。但王成心里不踏实，他觉得自己是个大男人，不能总靠姑妈养活。他想找点事做，挣点钱，也好在姑妈面前抬起头来。
姑妈看出他的心思，对他说：“成儿，你别急。我有个主意，你听听行不行。”
王成说：“姑妈请讲。”
姑妈说：“我年轻的时候，做过一阵子小买卖，攒下了一些绸缎。现在年纪大了，做不动了，一直放在柜子里，都快发霉了。你拿去卖掉，换些银子，做本钱，做点小生意。你祖上也是做官的，你不能总这么穷下去。”
王成听了，心里又酸又暖。他跪下来，给姑妈磕了三个头。“姑妈，你放心，我一定好好干，不给你丢人。”
姑妈从柜子里取出一匹绸缎，交给他。“这是上好的货，你拿去卖了，少说也能卖几十两银子。有了本钱，你就能翻身了。”
王成接过绸缎，千恩万谢。第二天一早，他背着绸缎，去了集市。
金陵的集市很热闹，人来人往，摩肩接踵。王成找了个地方，把绸缎摆出来，等着人来买。他等了一个上午，没有人问津。他急了，把价格降了又降，还是没人买。中午的时候，一个人走过来，看了看绸缎，又看了看王成，说：“这货是好货，但你卖的地方不对。这里都是些小商小贩，谁买得起这么贵的绸缎？你得去南市，那里才是卖好东西的地方。”
王成谢了那人，收拾了绸缎，往南市走。走到半路，忽然下起了大雨。他赶紧跑到一家店铺的屋檐下躲雨，把绸缎紧紧地抱在怀里，生怕淋湿了。雨越下越大，下了半个时辰还没停。王成站得腿都酸了，正要换个姿势，忽然看见对面街上走过来一个人。
那人穿着锦衣华服，气度不凡，一看就是有钱人。他走到王成面前，停下来，看了看他怀里的绸缎，说：“这货卖吗？”
王成连忙说：“卖卖卖。您出多少钱？”
那人摸了摸绸缎，说：“好货。我给你二十两银子，怎么样？”
王成大喜，二十两银子，比他预想的还多。他正要答应，忽然想起姑妈的话：“这货至少值五十两。”他犹豫了一下，说：“五十两。”
那人皱了皱眉，说：“太贵了。三十两。”
“四十两。”
“三十五两。不卖就算了。”
王成咬了咬牙，说：“好，三十五两。”
那人从袖中取出银子，递给王成，接过绸缎，转身走了。王成捧着银子，手都在发抖。他这辈子没见过这么多钱。他把银子揣进怀里，一路小跑回了姑妈家。
姑妈问他卖了多少钱，他说三十五两。姑妈叹了口气，说：“少了。那货至少值五十两。”王成低下头，说：“我……我着急了。”姑妈拍拍他的手，说：“没事，第一次做生意，难免的。有了本钱，下次就好了。”
content_en:
Chapter 12 Wang Cheng
After Song Tao finished reading "Promoting Weaving", he sat in front of the window for a long time. The moonlight shines in from the window and falls on the heavenly book, and the pages glow with a faint silver light. He thought about Cheng An, the cricket, and the wisp of smoke scattered in his father's palm. He thought for a long time, thinking about the moon setting in the west and the sky turning white. Finally he closed his eyes and fell asleep.
He had a dream. In the dream, he was standing on the edge of a large river. The river was so wide that he couldn't see the other side. There were many things floating on the river - paper boats, lanterns, and scattered books. He knelt down and reached for a piece of paper that floated over. There were words written on the paper, the ink was blurry, and I could barely make out a few: "Wang Cheng, a native of Pingyuan, lazy by nature, and from a poor family."
Before he could see clearly, the paper was washed away by the water. He stood up and looked upstream. Standing on the upper reaches of the river was an old man, wearing a shabby gown, with gray hair and a slightly hunched back. He was holding a pen in his hand - not a writing brush, but a very thin pen that looked like it was made of bone. The old man lowered his head and wrote on the river. When he writes a word, the river will turn and push the word downstream.
Song Tao wanted to walk over, but his feet couldn't move. He opened his mouth to ask, but no sound came out. The old man suddenly raised his head and glanced at him. At that glance, Song Tao felt that he had been seen through. It wasn't that his mind was read, but that everything was seen - every story he read and every celestial inscription he wrote was seen by the old man. It was like a book being turned to the last page and then closed.
The old man didn't speak, he lowered his head and continued writing. Song Tao stood on the shore and watched the words floating down from the upstream, one by one, densely packed and crowded together, like a school of fish competing for food. He saw a name - Wang Cheng. He reached for it and grabbed the paper. The paper was wet and the writing was blurry, but he could see it clearly.
He opened his eyes. It's daybreak. He was lying on the table with tears on his face. He lowered his head and looked at the Bible. The book opened and stopped at a new page.
This chapter is called "Wang Cheng".
There was an idle man named Wang Cheng in Pingyuan County. This man was originally a child of an aristocratic family. His ancestors had been high officials and his family was well off. But Wang Cheng was lazy by nature and not good at management, and his huge family fortune was completely ruined by him. By his generation, there were only a few shabby houses and a few acres of thin farmland left, and even eating was a problem. Wang Cheng was lazy and poor, but he didn't want to repent. He didn't get up until three o'clock in the morning every day. He didn't do anything when he got up. He just sat at the door to bask in the sun and watch the people coming and going on the street. Neighbors said that Wang Cheng's life was over.
Wang Cheng doesn't care. His parents died early, and no one cared about him. He could live however he wanted. Hungry and full, life flows like water, day by day, without any hope or worries.
This summer, Wang Cheng couldn't stay in the village any longer. He was so poor that he couldn't even afford porridge, so he had to seek refuge with relatives far away. He had an aunt who married in Jinling. She was widowed in her early years and her family was fairly well off. Wang Cheng thought of joining his aunt and making ends meet. He packed a bag, stuffed the few clothes he had into it, and some dry food, and set out on the road.
After walking for three days, halfway through, it got dark. With nowhere to go and nowhere to go, Wang Cheng had no choice but to rest in a dilapidated temple on the side of the road. He entered the temple, found a clean place, spread out his baggage, and lay down. Just as I was about to fall asleep, I suddenly heard a sound outside the door - "rustling", like someone rummaging through something.
He got up, leaned in the crack of the door and looked out. Under the moonlight, a man was squatting at the base of the wall, turning over a pile of broken bricks and tiles. The man rummaged for a while, took out a bunch of copper coins from the cracks in the bricks, counted them, put them in his arms, squatted down and continued to rummage.
Wang Cheng opened the door and walked out. The man was startled when he heard the noise, stood up and was about to run. Wang Cheng called out to him: "Brother, don't run. I'm not a bad person."
The man stopped, turned around, and glanced at him. He is a young man, in his early twenties, wearing shabby clothes, with a sallow face and thin muscles, like a beggar.
"Are you passing by?" the man asked.
"Yes." Wang Cheng said, "I'm going to Jinling to visit my relatives. What about you?"
The man sighed and said, "I also went to Jinling to visit my relatives. After walking for a day, I didn't eat anything and I was very hungry. I just dug out a few pennies under this wall and wanted to buy something to eat."
Wang Cheng felt sour, took out a piece of dry food from the bag and handed it over. "Eat."
The man was stunned for a moment, took the dry food, and ate it hungrily. After eating, he wiped his mouth and said, "Brother, you are a good man. My name is Li Sheng, and I am also from Pingyuan. We are traveling together, why don't we go together?"
Wang Cheng agreed. The two slept in the temple all night, got up early the next morning, and continued on their way.
After walking for five days, we arrived at Jinling. Wang Cheng found his aunt's house, and her aunt was surprised and happy to see him. She took Wang Cheng's hand, looked him up and down, and said, "Cheng'er, why are you so thin? Are you not eating enough at home?"
Wang Cheng was embarrassed to say so, he lowered his head and remained silent. The aunt sighed and packed a room for him to stay in. Wang Cheng stayed at his aunt's house for a few days. Her aunt was very kind to him. She made him delicious food every day and made him some new clothes. But Wang Cheng felt uneasy. He felt that he was a grown man and could not always rely on his aunt for support. He wanted to find something to do, earn some money, and look up in front of his aunt.
His aunt saw what he was thinking and said to him: "Cheng'er, don't worry. I have an idea. Do you think it's okay?"
Wang Cheng said: "Auntie, please speak."
The aunt said: "When I was young, I did a small business for a while and saved some silk and satin. Now that I am old, I can't do it anymore. It has been kept in the cabinet and is almost moldy. You can sell it and exchange it for some money to make capital and start a small business. Your ancestors were also officials, so you can't stay so poor forever."
Wang Cheng felt sour and warm in his heart after hearing this. He knelt down and kowtowed to his aunt three times. "Aunt, don't worry, I will do my job well and not embarrass you."
The aunt took out a piece of silk from the cabinet and handed it to him. "This is good quality goods. If you sell it, you can get it for dozens of taels of silver at least. With capital, you can turn around."
Wang Cheng took the silk and satin and thanked him profusely. Early the next morning, he carried the silk on his back and went to the market.
The market in Jinling is very lively, with people coming and going. Wang Cheng found a place and put the silks and satins out, waiting for people to buy them. He waited all morning, but no one cared. He was anxious and lowered the price again and again, but no one bought it. At noon, a man came over, looked at the silk and satin, then looked at Wang Cheng, and said: "This product is good, but you are selling it in the wrong place. There are all small traders here. Who can afford such expensive silk and satin? You have to go to Nanshi, that's where the good stuff is sold."
Wang Cheng thanked the man, packed up the silk and satin, and walked to Nanshi. Halfway through, it suddenly started raining heavily. He hurriedly ran to the eaves of a shop to take shelter from the rain, hugging the silk tightly in his arms for fear of getting wet. The rain got heavier and heavier, and it didn't stop for half an hour. Wang Cheng's legs were sore from standing. He was about to change his position when he suddenly saw a person walking across the street.
The man was dressed in rich clothes and had an extraordinary bearing. He looked like a rich man at first glance. He walked up to Wang Cheng, stopped, looked at the silk in his arms, and said, "Is this for sale?"
Wang Cheng quickly said: "Sell, sell, sell. How much do you want to pay?"
The man touched the silk and said, "Good stuff. How about I give you twenty taels of silver?"
Wang Cheng was overjoyed. Twenty taels of silver were more than he expected. He was about to agree when he suddenly remembered his aunt's words: "This thing is worth at least fifty taels." He hesitated and said, "Fifty taels."
The man frowned and said, "It's too expensive. Thirty taels."
"Forty taels."
"Thirty-five taels. Forget it if you don't sell it."
Wang Cheng gritted his teeth and said, "Okay, thirty-five taels."
The man took out the silver from his sleeve, handed it to Wang Cheng, took the silk and satin, and turned away. Wang Cheng held the silver, his hands trembling. He had never seen so much money in his life. He put the silver in his arms and ran back to his aunt's house.
The aunt asked him how much he sold it for, and he said thirty-five taels. The aunt sighed and said, "It's missing. That item is worth at least fifty taels." Wang Cheng lowered his head and said, "I...I'm anxious." The aunt patted his hand and said, "It's okay. It's inevitable when you do business for the first time. If you have the capital, it will be fine next time."
